# Construction and Application of a Sports Intelligent Tutoring and Learning Guidance System Driven by Multimodal Data Fusion

The evidence supports constructing such a system, but not claiming that one fully validated, universally applicable system already exists. The strongest evidence supports a modular, human-supervised system that combines video or pose, inertial and motion sensing, physiological data, expert assessment, learner history, and contextual information to estimate skill state, provide feedback, and adapt training. Recent systems have demonstrated technically credible results: a school physical-education prototype reached 91.3 ± 0.4% agreement with teacher scoring and 43.2 ms inference latency; EdgeFusionNet achieved 91.8 ± 0.7% recognition accuracy in uncontrolled table-tennis sessions and a 10.3-percentage-point hit-rate advantage over a matched control after four weeks; and a track-and-field intervention reported faster proficiency and lower injury likelihood under a randomized design. These outcomes remain task- and population-specific, however, and do not establish autonomous coaching or universal learning transfer. [BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation prototype](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13102-026-01792-9) [EdgeFusionNet](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-58591-y) [track-and-field intervention](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-20745-9)

This report therefore defines the requested Sports Intelligent Tutoring and Learning Guidance System (SITLGS) as a reference architecture and application model grounded in existing evidence. Its proper role is to make sports learning more observable, individualized, timely, and explainable while retaining teacher or coach responsibility for interpretation, safety, motivation, and high-stakes decisions. The available literature is rich in recognition models, datasets, prototypes, and vendor capabilities, but thinner in independent longitudinal validation, cross-sport transfer, coach-workload measurement, cost analysis, and sustained attributable educational outcomes.

The report resolves seven questions in sequence. It first defines the system and its pedagogical foundation; then compares research prototypes, datasets, institutional initiatives, and commercial products. It specifies users and data requirements, describes a complete construction architecture, explains practical tutoring workflows, establishes an evaluation framework, analyzes deployment and governance, and concludes with a staged implementation roadmap and research agenda.

## 1. Study objective, scope, and conceptual foundation

### 1.1 Objective and system definition

The study objective is to determine how a sports intelligent tutoring and learning-guidance system can be constructed from multimodal data and applied across sports education, athlete development, coaching, training, rehabilitation support, and institutional physical-education settings.

The proposed system is a closed-loop socio-technical system with seven functions:

1. acquire multimodal evidence about movement, physiology, learning activity, context, and self-reported experience;
2. align, clean, and quality-check those data;
3. infer actions, technique features, fatigue or readiness indicators, and learner state;
4. compare observed performance with sport-specific domain knowledge and individualized goals;
5. generate feedback, practice recommendations, and alerts;
6. record responses and progress over time;
7. route uncertain, unsafe, or context-sensitive decisions to a coach, teacher, clinician, or other authorized human.

The exact named system has not been defined and validated as one integrated artifact in the retrieved evidence. This is an important boundary. The report does not present the system as an existing product or as a result already demonstrated in one trial. Instead, it synthesizes validated components and proposes how they should be integrated.

The problem context is familiar across sports. Conventional physical education often relies on teacher observation, fixed teaching sequences, manual scoring, and delayed correction. Large classes limit the time available for individualized instruction. In high-performance sport, coaches may have access to extensive data but still face fragmented devices, delayed analysis, poor interoperability, and difficulty translating numerical outputs into actionable instruction. The 2026 smart physical-education classroom study explicitly identifies delayed movement correction and limited individualization as the problems its cloud-edge-end design attempts to address. [Smart physical-education classroom system](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01082-w)

The SITLGS is intended for five user groups:

- athletes and sports learners, who need understandable feedback, practice guidance, progress information, and safe adaptation;
- coaches, who need decision support, individualized training recommendations, and efficient review;
- physical-education teachers, who need formative assessment, class-level monitoring, and support for differentiated instruction;
- sport-science, rehabilitation, and support staff, who need longitudinal, multimodal evidence and uncertainty-aware alerts;
- administrators, who need information about participation, learning progress, equipment, safety, equity, and resource use.

Administrator-specific workflows and acceptance criteria are not adequately documented in the retrieved evidence. This is a genuine gap rather than a reason to omit administrators from the system boundary. Their requirements must be established locally before procurement or deployment.

The scope is global and cross-sport, covering research prototypes, datasets, institutional initiatives, deployed systems, commercial products, construction methods, instructional applications, evaluation, deployment, and governance through 13 September 2026. Examples include school PE, individual technical sports, team sports, endurance training, youth sport, rehabilitation, and adaptive exercise. The system is not assumed to be a medical diagnostic device. If it processes health data or contributes to rehabilitation or return-to-sport decisions, it requires the additional clinical, regulatory, and professional controls appropriate to that use.

### 1.2 The pedagogical problem: from measurement to learning

A sports tutoring system must do more than classify an action. Classification answers “what happened?” Tutoring must also address:

- what the learner was trying to do;
- which component was performed inadequately;
- why that component matters;
- what practice should follow;
- how difficult the next task should be;
- whether the learner is ready to progress;
- how feedback should be timed and expressed;
- when the system should defer to a human.

This distinction separates intelligent tutoring from conventional sports analytics and fitness tracking.

| System type | Primary purpose | Typical output | Main limitation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Conventional sports analytics | Describe performance, tactics, workload, or competition events | Dashboards, statistics, clips, rankings, forecasts | Often does not model learning or prescribe instructional steps |
| Fitness tracking | Monitor activity, physiological state, or adherence | Steps, heart rate, sleep, strain, recovery, reminders | Usually uses generic goals and limited technique diagnosis |
| Multimodal learning analytics | Relate several data streams to learning indicators | Engagement, cognition, emotion, collaboration, performance indicators | May identify learning states without delivering instruction |
| Intelligent tutoring | Estimate learner state and adapt instruction or feedback | Error explanations, task selection, scaffolding, progress guidance | Requires a domain model, learner model, pedagogical policy, and communication design |
| Sports SITLGS | Combine all four functions in sport-specific contexts | Timely technique feedback, adaptive practice, safety-aware plans, coach support | Evidence for complete, cross-sport, long-term systems remains limited |

The distinction is consistent with the psychomotor intelligent-tutoring literature. Romano and colleagues describe an ITS as a combination of domain, student, tutor, and communication models. Their review identifies sport examples in dance, badminton, yoga, and fitness, but finds that most existing psychomotor ITS support fine, closed, internally paced, discrete, individual, and relatively simple skills. Gross, open, strength, flexibility, and affective learning remain underrepresented. [Romano et al.’s systematic review of psychomotor ITS](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40593-025-00526-1)

The system should therefore be designed around learning progression rather than only output recognition. Harrow’s psychomotor taxonomy, used in the same review, distinguishes reflex movements, basic fundamental movements, perceptual abilities, physical abilities, skilled movements, and non-discursive communication. Sport instruction also varies along granularity, environmental openness, pace, continuity, interactivity, and complexity. These dimensions matter because a model that works for an isolated badminton stroke may fail in a contested football situation or a changing outdoor environment.

### 1.3 Theoretical foundation

#### Intelligent tutoring systems

The four ITS models provide the minimum conceptual structure.

The domain model represents the sport: movement phases, technical criteria, tactical rules, safety constraints, progressions, common errors, and acceptable individual variation. For example, a table-tennis domain model may encode stroke preparation, racket path, timing, contact, recovery, and footwork. A track-and-field model may distinguish sprint-start mechanics from acceleration-phase mechanics, an error that the track-and-field system reported as a principal source of confusion.

The learner model represents the individual: current mastery, prior experience, physical and psychological state, goals, preferences, recent workload, error history, confidence, and response to previous feedback. It should be longitudinal and individualized rather than based only on a population average.

The tutor model selects instructional actions. It determines whether to demonstrate, explain, ask a reflective question, prescribe a drill, reduce difficulty, increase challenge, delay feedback, or request human review.

The communication model determines how the guidance is delivered. Visual overlays, color-coded joint trajectories, voice, text, haptic signals, augmented reality, or a coach dashboard are not interchangeable. Their appropriateness depends on sport, learner age, sensory access, attention, environment, and task phase.

#### Motor learning and skill acquisition

The system should use motor-learning principles to decide not only whether feedback is correct but whether it is educationally useful. Feedback that arrives too late may help retrospective understanding but fail to support immediate movement correction. Feedback that is too frequent or too detailed may overload the learner and reduce self-regulation.

The challenge-point perspective suggests that the value of a task depends on the interaction between learner skill, task difficulty, and available information. A beginner may need a simple external cue, whereas an advanced athlete may benefit from a constraint, comparison, or question that encourages self-discovery. Ecological-dynamics perspectives similarly caution against treating one technically ideal movement as universally correct. The system should identify useful constraints and risks while allowing adaptations to body structure, environment, and tactical intention.

The 2024 speed-skating study explicitly connected AI-assisted instruction with Self-Determination Theory, Social Cognitive Theory, mastery-climate research, the Challenge Point Framework, and ecological dynamics. Its interpretation was that competence-supportive feedback and successful correction can strengthen motivation and self-efficacy, although the mediation evidence was statistical rather than definitive causal proof. [Speed-skating intervention](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12907373/)

#### Self-Determination Theory

Self-Determination Theory (SDT) identifies autonomy, competence, and relatedness as basic psychological needs. These principles have direct design implications.

Autonomy means allowing learners to choose devices, timing, goals, practice variants, and in some cases feedback intensity. Competence means matching difficulty to current capability, showing understandable progress, and avoiding feedback that merely announces failure. Relatedness means preserving connection with teachers, coaches, peers, and supportive human relationships.

The Lexue 100 study is not evidence for multimodal sports-skill tutoring: it was an academic mathematics-and-English ITS used by 33 adolescent student-athletes. It is nevertheless relevant to the pedagogical design problem. Its pilot identified inflexible technology, missing identity, and mismatched difficulty as barriers. The redesign offered device choice, access to real teachers, a supportive virtual character, and Item Response Theory-based difficulty adaptation. Completion rose from 21.2% to 72.7% in mathematics and from 55.7% to 90.9% in English, while academic motivation increased significantly; the different questions used in the two stages mean that the accuracy increase requires caution. [SDT-based ITS for student-athletes](https://doi.org/10.3390/su152014709)

For a sports tutor, SDT implies that an algorithm should not simply maximize compliance. It should help learners understand and influence their development. A recommendation that lowers training load may support safety but undermine autonomy if presented as an unchallengeable command. A system that displays every deviation may increase surveillance and anxiety. Human coaches remain necessary to interpret motivation, relationships, identity, and context.

#### Behavioral Skills Training and reflective learning

Behavioral Skills Training (BST) provides a practical sequence for teaching observable skills: instruction, modeling, rehearsal, and feedback. ViSTAR, an augmented-reality basketball system, uses this structure. It reconstructs motion in three dimensions, identifies salient differences through model decision paths, and uses a language model to turn those differences into verbal cues. Its formative evaluation involved five university players, two coaches, and two user studies with a total of 16 participants. Participants generally preferred the generated feedback or found it useful for noticing posture and balance issues, but the small, short-term design does not establish performance improvement. [ViSTAR](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.22077v2)

The design lesson is that an LLM should not be treated as the source of biomechanical truth. It should verbalize structured, validated findings from the domain and learner models. The Frontiers ITS framework that combines video transcripts and textbook PDFs illustrates a similar principle: a knowledge graph and retrieval layer are used to ground language-model responses, while expert validation remains necessary because automatic graph enrichment can introduce hallucinations or domain errors. [Multimodal knowledge-graph ITS](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/computer-science/articles/10.3389/fcomp.2026.1777749/full)

#### Multimodal learning analytics

The multimodal learning-analytics literature provides the bridge between sensor fusion and pedagogy. A systematic review classifies learning data into digital, physical, physiological, psychometric, and environmental spaces. Its learning indicators include behavior, cognition, emotion, collaboration, and engagement. It proposes a three-stage process:

1. acquire learning-process data;
2. map multimodal data to learning indicators;
3. use the resulting understanding to improve learning performance.

The framework also distinguishes data, indicator, theory, and technology layers. This is important because raw acceleration, heart rate, or gaze does not automatically mean “poor motivation,” “fatigue,” or “understanding.” Such meanings require pedagogical and psychological theory, validated operational definitions, and cautious interpretation. [Multimodal Data Fusion in Learning Analytics](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7729570/)

A 2026 systems survey gives a closely related six-stage architecture: data acquisition and temporal alignment, preprocessing, modality-specific feature extraction, multimodal fusion, modeling and inference, and pedagogical interpretation. It also warns that studies frequently under-specify synchronization, missing data, fusion procedures, deployment conditions, and ethics. [Future Internet survey of multimodal learning analytics](https://doi.org/10.3390/fi18030115)

### 1.4 Research process and evidence status

This report uses a structured narrative synthesis of the supplied scholarly studies, datasets, technical papers, reviews, official guidance, and official product descriptions. The source strategy covered:

- the exact system concept and sports ITS terminology;
- psychomotor tutoring, learner models, adaptive feedback, and SDT;
- video, pose, IMU, physiological, audio, text, and self-report fusion;
- early, intermediate, late, and hybrid fusion;
- edge-cloud deployment, real-time feedback, and interoperability;
- representative products such as Sportsbox AI, WHOOP AI Guidance, and Hudl;
- learning gains, retention, transfer, adherence, safety, coach acceptance, and workload;
- privacy, biometrics, minors, fairness, explainability, and cybersecurity.

Included evidence comprises controlled and quasi-experimental studies, field deployments, dataset and benchmark papers, systematic and scoping reviews, conceptual and architectural studies, government and sport-governance guidance, and vendor descriptions when the requirement concerned reported capability rather than effectiveness. Retrieved pages that contained only “Redirecting” or a 404 response were not treated as substantive evidence.

Evidence status is reported explicitly:

- intervention evidence: comparative or longitudinal studies involving learners or athletes;
- field validation: systems evaluated under realistic operating conditions;
- technical validation: datasets, held-out tests, robustness experiments, or latency evaluations;
- framework evidence: proposed architectures or design principles;
- capability evidence: official product descriptions without independent quantitative evaluation;
- governance evidence: legal, regulatory, or institutional requirements.

The report-specific final database list, search log, deduplication counts, screening counts, final search date, and formal quality appraisal of every included source are unavailable in the supplied material. Accordingly, this is not presented as a new fully reproducible systematic review. It is an evidence-grounded design and application study that uses the transparent methods and limitations reported by the supplied reviews. For example, Romano et al. synthesized 122 psychomotor-ITS papers, the Bioengineering scoping review included 73 sports-biomechanics studies, and a 2026 sports-AI scoping review included 32 publications but only 10 fully verified primary empirical studies. [Bioengineering scoping review](https://doi.org/10.3390/bioengineering12080887) [Sports-AI scoping review](https://ijpefs.org/index.php/ijpefs/article/view/833)

## 2. Existing research, prototypes, and representative systems

### 2.1 Evidence landscape

Existing systems occupy different positions on a progression:

1. sensing and recognition;
2. assessment against expert or rubric labels;
3. feedback generation;
4. adaptive tutoring;
5. measurable learning improvement;
6. sustained, cross-context deployment.

Many papers establish only the first two levels. Some add feedback or recommendation generation. A smaller group includes controlled educational outcomes. Very few demonstrate all levels together with independent external validation, retention, transfer, cost, safety, and coach-workload evidence.

The systems below should therefore not be interpreted as a league table. Their purposes, sports, populations, labels, and endpoints differ too greatly for a single ranking to be valid.

### 2.2 Research systems and institutional initiatives

| System and evidence status | Sport, users, and context | Modalities and fusion | Tutoring or deployment function | Reported evidence and limits |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Smart physical-education classroom; proposed and experimentally verified | College students; basketball, gymnastics, long-distance running | Cameras, IMUs, heart rate, voice; three-tier cloud-edge-end architecture | Edge recognition and instant feedback; cloud analysis and training prescription | 45 adults; 89.4–93.2% recognition, 176–180 ms edge response, 4.3–4.6 satisfaction; no controlled learning-transfer result |
| Multimodal PE assessment model; technical and pedagogical prototype | 245 middle-school students in three schools; basketball dribbling, standing long jump, sit-ups, 50 m sprint | Seven IMU nodes plus digitized teacher rubric; DTW, hierarchical attention, gated fusion | Formative assessment and teacher decision support | 3,920 samples; 91.3 ± 0.4% agreement with teacher scoring; 43.2 ms inference; external cohort validation remains absent |
| CoachXNet; proposed edge-cloud platform | Athletes represented in SportsPose and AthletePose3D | 17 IMUs, optical motion capture, GPS; edge CNN/RNN, cloud GCN/Transformer, attention fusion | Voice, AR, and haptic feedback; injury-risk and workload modules | Reported 94.1% accuracy, 35.2 mm MPJPE, 32 ms latency, and 18–23% individualized-training advantage, but the same source also reports 94.6%, 92.8%, and 27.8 ms; no field deployment result |
| EdgeFusionNet; field-validated research prototype | Table-tennis athletes in gymnasium training | High-speed vision, IMU, sEMG; cross-modal attention, compression, adaptive offloading | Stroke recognition and actionable low-latency feedback | 93.6 ± 0.4% laboratory accuracy, 90.4 ± 2.3% leave-one-subject-out, 91.8 ± 0.7% field accuracy; 10.3-point hit-rate advantage after four weeks; independent multi-site validation remains needed |
| Track-and-field intelligent teaching framework; randomized intervention | 312 undergraduates aged 18–24 in three university athletic centers | Cameras, IMUs, force platforms, meteorological stations; CNN-BiLSTM, XGBoost/MLP, Bayesian RNN, Random Forest, constrained MDP | Technique classification, performance prediction, injury-risk classification, adaptive content sequencing | 16-week comparison; optimized group reached proficiency 27.3% faster and reported 41.2% lower injury likelihood; source-specific outcomes require replication |
| PoseSync Vitality; randomized educational trial | 120 undergraduates in a compulsory university Tai Chi course | Pose-estimation video; comparison with video instruction | Real-time movement feedback, joint-specific cues, summaries | Larger gains and higher personalization ratings than video instruction, including a two-week retention test; exact effect sizes are unavailable in the supplied evidence |
| REVERIE; randomized VR sports-health system | Adolescents with excess body weight learning soccer and table tennis | VR, expert templates, deep reinforcement learning, transformer agent, heart-rate telemetry | Empathetic virtual technique guidance and human-coach schedule support | Main text reports 240 enrolled, 96/96/48 allocation, eight weeks, >90% compliance, and six-month gains; abstract reports 227, creating a sample discrepancy |
| SpeedSkate-AI condition; quasi-experimental field study | 129 first-year middle-school speed skaters in China | Two fixed cameras; teacher-mediated video feedback | Scheduled technique feedback within lessons | Eight weeks; 500 m improvement exceeded conventional teaching; intact classes confounded teaching mode with class context |
| BoxingPro; prototype and expert evaluation | 18 volunteers aged 5–40, including novices and professionals | Two hand IMUs plus 200-FPS video; pose estimation and LLM prompt generation | Sequential punch-specific feedback | 324 paired punch instances; professional-boxer rating exceeded 4/5 for correctness and actionability; no longitudinal learning comparison |
| Multimodal Tutor and CPR Tutor; doctoral prototype | Psychomotor learners, especially CPR trainees | Kinematic and myographic data; supervised neural networks | Real-time adaptive feedback from machine assessment | Establishes a psychomotor tutoring architecture and case study; not a sports intervention and not evidence of cross-sport transfer |

The [smart physical-education system](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01082-w) demonstrates the practical logic of separating low-latency inference from long-term analysis. Cameras operate at 30 Hz, IMUs at 100 Hz, and Polar H10 heart-rate straps at 1 Hz. The system reports filtering, interpolation, transcript-confidence screening, normalization, and a long-term performance index that maps to 3–5 training items. The main experiment involved 45 healthy adults, and the results are therefore better understood as technical feasibility and user acceptance than as evidence of school learning transfer.

The [BMC PE model](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13102-026-01792-9) provides a stronger assessment example. It collected 3,920 skill samples from 245 students across three schools and four sports. Six MTw Awinda IMUs and an additional waist node sampled at 100 Hz, while a tablet digitized a four-tier teacher rubric. DTW addressed the mismatch between continuous sensor data and discrete teacher scores; attention and gated fusion adjusted the relative contribution of each modality according to data quality. The model reproduced expert-level teacher scoring, not an objective biomechanical truth. This distinction is central: a system can be highly consistent with teachers while inheriting their rubric assumptions and biases.

[EdgeFusionNet](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-58591-y) is among the strongest direct demonstrations of multimodal, edge-cloud, real-time sports feedback in the supplied evidence. It combines vision, IMU, and sEMG, uses hardware-triggered synchronization, compresses a cloud model for edge execution, and uses Q-learning to decide whether computation should occur locally or in the cloud. The field result is important because recognition remained high under uncontrolled gymnasium conditions and the study included a matched control comparison. It still concerns one sport, seven canonical stroke types, and 30 training sessions; it does not establish transfer to team sports, young children, outdoor settings, or other learning objectives.

[CoachXNet](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44196-025-01146-2) illustrates both architectural ambition and reporting risk. Its parallel edge and cloud paths are appropriate for a system that must react within a motion cycle while retaining richer longitudinal modeling. The same paper, however, reports conflicting accuracy and latency values without explaining whether they refer to different datasets or experimental conditions. Those values should therefore be retained as reported estimates rather than treated as a reliable benchmark.

The [track-and-field framework](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-20745-9) advances beyond recognition by connecting technique, prediction, injury-risk classification, and content optimization. Its constrained Markov decision process defines learner knowledge profiles as states, teaching interventions as actions, and performance or knowledge gains as rewards. This is conceptually close to a sports tutor, but the model’s impressive reported outcomes require replication because one controlled study cannot establish universal injury or learning effects.

### 2.3 Psychomotor tutoring and feedback systems

The [Multimodal Tutor thesis](https://research.ou.nl/en/publications/the-multimodal-tutor-adaptive-feedback-from-multimodal-experience) provides an important historical bridge. Its CPR Tutor captures kinematic and myographic information, uses human-annotated samples to train supervised models, assesses task execution, and produces adaptive real-time feedback. The contribution is not a sports product but a general psychomotor tutoring pattern that can be adapted to sport.

The [T3Set table-tennis dataset and virtual-coach framework](https://doi.org/10.1145/3711896.3737407) addresses a problem that video alone cannot solve. Strength and acceleration details require sensing, while coaching suggestions require domain knowledge and language. T3Set synchronizes racket IMU data with video for 32 players, covers seven techniques and 380 training rounds, and contains 8,655 annotated strokes with 8,395 coach-targeted suggestions. The associated two-stage system connects motion perception to an LLM-based virtual coach. It is a valuable foundation for tutoring, but the dataset and framework do not by themselves demonstrate retention, transfer, or safe autonomous instruction.

The [PoseSync Vitality trial](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10639-026-14132-8) is significant because it compares AI-supported Tai Chi instruction with video instruction under the same curriculum and practice dose. Expert instructors rated performance at pretest, posttest, and two-week retention. The supplied evidence reports larger performance gains, greater interface and personalization ratings, and higher posttest consistency in the AI group, but not the exact numerical effect sizes. It supports the proposition that real-time pose-based feedback can improve short-term learning conditions; it does not establish that the system can generalize to open, interactive sports.

The [REVERIE system](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1038/s41591-025-03724-5) places tutoring within a wider health and motivation intervention. It uses expert coaching templates, deep reinforcement learning, transformer-based virtual agents, VR, sport-specific interfaces, and heart-rate telemetry. In the main-text account of its three-arm trial, the REVERIE sports group reduced fat mass by 4.28 kg relative to control, had minimal injuries in 7.69% of participants, and maintained improvements in standing long jump, self-efficacy, well-being, sleep, eating behavior, and sports willingness at six months. Those outcomes support engagement and health-related application, but the sample discrepancy between the abstract and main text must be reported rather than silently resolved.

The [ViSTAR basketball system](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.22077v2) demonstrates a different tutoring route: observable movement is translated into language through a Random Forest decision path and an LLM. It is explicitly grounded in BST and uses 3D avatars, overlays, rhythm cues, and timing cues. Its small formative sample suggests acceptability and perceived usefulness, not demonstrated performance gain.

The evidence is more mature for closed technical tasks than for open tactical learning. Badminton tutors reviewed by Romano et al. provide visual feedback, similarity scores, and novice–expert comparisons for serving, smashing, clearing, and backhand driving. Dance tutors provide rhythm and posture feedback. Yoga systems measure pose or joint-angle differences. These tasks have clear movement episodes and relatively stable reference structures. In football, basketball, hockey, and other open sports, the same observed posture may be appropriate or inappropriate depending on opponent, space, timing, and tactical intention.

### 2.4 Commercial systems and capability evidence

| Product | Sport and users | Reported inputs or modalities | Reported tutoring functions | Evidence boundary |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sportsbox AI | Golfers and golf coaches | Product page reports 3D swing analysis; sensor details are not specified | Set goals, receive feedback on every swing, track progress, ask AI chat about swing and next steps | Vendor capability description; no supplied sample, accuracy, fusion architecture, integration specification, or learning outcome |
| WHOOP AI Guidance | WHOOP members seeking health and performance guidance | HRV, sleep, strain, Recovery, goals, routines, and user context; LLM interaction | Real-time personalized recommendations and conversational guidance | Vendor reports a beta wellness tool, not medical advice; no independent audit or sports-learning outcome in supplied evidence |
| Hudl | Coaches, teams, groups, and individual athletes across sports | Video libraries, data, clips, annotations, comments, drawings, messaging | Review, presentation, individualized video feedback, team communication | Strong workflow and video-communication capability; no supplied sensor fusion, tutoring model, or controlled learning outcome |
| Vmaxpro and related products | Professional soccer trainers and athletes | Body-worn IMU in the cited example | Smartphone training recommendations and strength exercises | Product example cited in a benchmark paper; no supplied quantitative tutoring or multimodal outcome |
| SIQ sensor-equipped basketball | Basketball players | Instrumented ball | Shooting feedback | Product example; no supplied independent evaluation or integration evidence |

[Sportsbox AI](https://www.sportsbox.ai/) presents a clear commercial learning sequence—measure, set a goal, practice with feedback, and track progress with AI chat. The page does not reveal the sensor configuration, fusion strategy, integration requirements, or outcome evidence. It should therefore be treated as a capability example, not as validation of multimodal intelligent tutoring.

[WHOOP AI Guidance](https://www.whoop.com/us/en/thelocker/new-ai-guidance-from-whoop/) combines continuous biometric data with user context and a fine-tuned language model. WHOOP states that the tool is in beta, intended for informational and wellness use, and not a substitute for medical diagnosis or treatment. It also describes consent-based access and anonymization before a third-party language-model partner processes metrics. These are company-reported controls, not independent audit findings. The system is closer to adaptive wellness guidance than to sport-skill tutoring because the supplied description contains no video, technique model, or instructional curriculum.

[Hudl](https://www.hudl.com/en_gb/products/hudl) illustrates the value of workflow integration. Coaches can create playlists, presentations, annotated clips, and individualized feedback inside an established team platform. Its practical strength is communication and review rather than demonstrated multimodal inference. A SITLGS should learn from this emphasis: a technically strong model that does not fit existing coaching routines may be less useful than a simpler model embedded in a coach’s normal workflow.

## 3. Users, pedagogical needs, and multimodal data requirements

### 3.1 User roles and decisions

| User | Main tasks | Required system outputs | Human decision authority | Evidence gap |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Athlete or learner | Practice, self-assess, respond to feedback, set goals, monitor progress | Understandable errors, demonstrations, next drills, confidence, progress, safety prompts | Accept, question, or ignore ordinary guidance; report symptoms and context | Accessibility and learner-control requirements vary widely |
| Coach | Plan, observe, individualize, review, manage load, communicate | Player profiles, technique summaries, uncertainty, recommended drills, workload trends, alerts | Final technical, tactical, load, and motivational decisions | Sustained coach-workload and acceptance evidence is limited |
| PE teacher | Teach classes, assess, differentiate, give formative feedback | Class dashboard, rubric-linked assessment, disagreement flags, group patterns | Override scores, adapt instruction, protect student welfare | Administrator and school-level workflows remain under-specified |
| Sport scientist or rehabilitation staff | Validate measures, monitor risk, interpret recovery | Longitudinal multimodal trends, calibration, uncertainty, reference comparisons | Professional assessment and escalation | Clinical translation and prospective safety evidence remain limited |
| Administrator | Procure, govern, allocate resources, monitor participation and equity | Adoption, cost, data-governance, uptime, accessibility, safety, and outcome reports | Institutional policy, contracts, retention, and accountability | Retrieved studies rarely define administrator requirements or acceptance criteria |

A useful design principle follows: different users should not receive the same dashboard. Athletes need concise, actionable guidance. Coaches need comparisons and uncertainty. Teachers need rubric-linked explanations and class-level patterns. Administrators need governance and resource information rather than raw physiological traces.

### 3.2 Learning tasks and sport contexts

The system should distinguish at least four instructional contexts.

Closed individual skills include Tai Chi, yoga, isolated boxing punches, golf swings, badminton strokes, and some gymnastics elements. They are relatively suitable for pose comparison, temporal segmentation, reference trajectories, and immediate corrective cues.

Periodic or repetitive tasks include sit-ups, running, cycling, rowing, and swimming. Here, fatigue, rhythm, repetition quality, and load-response patterns are important. A system may need to summarize a session rather than interrupt every repetition.

Open interactive skills include football, basketball, volleyball, hockey, and handball. The environment, opponent, teammates, tactical objectives, and available space influence whether a movement is appropriate. A model trained on isolated movements should not issue categorical technique judgments during open play without context.

Rehabilitation and return-to-sport tasks require additional clinical constraints. The objective is not simply to maximize performance. It is to monitor compensations, pain or symptom reports, loading tolerance, confidence, and readiness while leaving medical decisions to qualified professionals.

Age and ability also change requirements. Children and adolescents need stronger consent, safety, accessibility, and developmental safeguards. Para-athletes may require individualized movement models rather than normative “ideal” patterns. A perspective on AI and disability inclusion argues that assistive devices, wearables, and data-driven rehabilitation can improve accessibility and personalization, but also warns about privacy, algorithmic bias, and overreliance on technology. [AI and sports inclusion for persons with disabilities](https://doi.org/10.22271/kheljournal.2026.v13.i4e.4452)

### 3.3 Data modalities

| Modality | Typical variables | Instructional value | Typical risks or quality problems |
|---|---|---|---|
| Video and pose | Frames, keypoints, joint angles, trajectories, object or ball position, gaze | Technique, posture, timing, coordination, tactical context, visual demonstration | Occlusion, lighting, viewpoint, privacy, computational cost, identity leakage |
| Inertial and motion sensing | Acceleration, angular velocity, orientation, displacement, GPS, UWB, force, pressure | Movement phase, load, speed, stability, asymmetry, fatigue-related mechanics | Drift, misalignment, placement changes, synchronization, battery and comfort |
| Physiological and biochemical | HR, HRV, ECG, SpO₂, respiration, skin temperature, EMG, sweat lactate, electrolytes | Internal load, readiness, fatigue, recovery, exertion, stress | Motion artefacts, individual baselines, sensor contact, calibration, health-data sensitivity |
| Audio and speech | Voice commands, coach comments, learner questions, self-talk, transcripts | Conversational tutoring, explanation, reflection, coach annotation | Noise, speaker diarization, accents, domain terminology, consent |
| Text, self-report, and psychometric data | Goals, perceived exertion, pain, fatigue, sleep, mood, motivation, confidence, reflections | Contextualization, motivation, subjective state, learner preferences | Recall bias, missingness, social desirability, sensitivity, subjective interpretation |
| Environmental and contextual data | Weather, temperature, humidity, wind, surface, venue, equipment, competition phase, role, opponent, schedule | Context-aware adaptation, environmental correction, tactical interpretation | Location privacy, confounding, missing context, cross-site shift |
| Institutional and learning traces | Rubric scores, attendance, completion, practice history, LMS interactions, coach feedback | Mastery modeling, progression, adherence, teacher support | Data ownership, incompatible systems, administrative misuse |

The 2021 multimodal learning-analytics review identifies physical, physiological, psychometric, environmental, and digital spaces as complementary. It includes eye movement, facial expression, audio, posture, location, EEG, EDA, ECG, PPG, HR/HRV, respiration, motivation questionnaires, weather, clickstreams, and learning artifacts. The classification is useful for sports because it prevents “multimodal” from being reduced to video plus one wearable. [MMLA review](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7729570/)

### 3.4 Representative datasets and their instructional relevance

| Dataset or resource | Context and population | Modalities | Labels or guidance | Status and limitation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MultiSenseBadminton | 25 players, 7,763 swings, beginner to expert | Eye tracking, body tracking, EMG, foot pressure, video, surveys, interviews | Stroke type, skill level, sound, landing, hitting location; coach-informed criteria | Strong multimodal foundation; controlled individual strokes do not represent unpredictable matches |
| T3Set | 32 table-tennis players, 380 rounds | Racket IMU at 100 Hz, video, coach text | 8,655 strokes and 8,395 coach suggestions | Supports motion-to-language tutoring; does not establish longitudinal learning |
| Hang-Time HAR | 24 basketball participants from teams in the United States and Germany | Wrist inertial data, video-supported labels | Four label layers and multiple activity classes | Includes drills and naturalistic games; lacks successful-scoring information for direct skill assessment |
| FLEX | 38 subjects, more than 7,500 recordings, 20 loaded exercises | RGB, 3D pose, sEMG, physiological signals | Fine-grained action-quality labels and a fitness knowledge graph | Strong coaching foundation; not a reported longitudinal tutoring intervention |
| MM-Fit | Full-body exercise participants across 10 exercises | RGB/depth video, accelerometer, gyroscope, magnetometer, heart rate | Activity segmentation and exercise recognition | Five time-synchronized devices; tutoring outcomes are not reported |
| SportSkills | 638,399 paired clips from 369,296 videos across 55 sports | Instructional video and narration | Actionability and visual demonstration judgments | Broad weakly supervised resource; inventory totals differ across sections and it emphasizes visual single-person skills |

[MultiSenseBadminton](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-024-03144-z) is notable because its sensor design was informed by interviews with three professional badminton coaches. The coaches emphasized grip, posture, swing, footwork, impact point, trajectory, accuracy, sound, and speed. They also recognized that video may not communicate force or center-of-gravity concepts equally well to every learner. This is exactly the kind of expert knowledge a domain model must preserve rather than replace.

MultiSenseBadminton uses Unix timestamps, TCP/IP or stream-layer APIs, HDF5 storage, five wearable-sensor types, three cameras, and a shuttlecock launcher. Its acquisition continued when a sensor disconnected, illustrating a practical principle: the system should degrade gracefully and record which modality was unavailable rather than silently treating missing data as valid.

[Hang-Time HAR](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10346876/) demonstrates ecological variability. The recordings include controlled warm-ups and drills as well as uncontrolled games, and participants differ in gender, body dimensions, play style, fatigue, stress, and skill. The United States and Germany recordings also reflect different rule systems and court dimensions. The paper reports both 10 activities in its summary and 15 classes in its table; that inconsistency should be preserved in any catalogue and resolved before benchmarking.

[FLEX](https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2506.03198) connects sensing to instructional knowledge through a Fitness Knowledge Graph linking actions, steps, error types, and feedback. This is a useful design model for the SITLGS domain layer. [MM-Fit](https://mmfit.github.io/) provides a simpler example of multimodal representation learning: modality-specific autoencoders produce representations that are combined into a shared cross-modal representation before activity classification.

[SportSkills](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.25163v1) provides scale but not yet educational validation. Its table reports 57,314 hours, 349,141 videos, 220,761 participants, 1,702 skills, and 55 domains, while the implementation description reports 369,296 downloaded videos and 638,399 clips. Manual checks of 200 language-model labels found 95% correctness, and 200 visual-language outputs achieved 91% agreement with the authors. Training improved retrieval or representation metrics in 52 of 55 sports, but the resource evaluates video representation and feedback relevance rather than learner retention or transfer.

### 3.5 Data quality, synchronization, and labeling requirements

A deployable system needs explicit requirements for:

- clock synchronization and timestamp provenance;
- sensor placement and calibration;
- packet loss and battery state;
- missingness and failure-mode classification;
- participant-wise data splitting;
- annotation protocol and rater reliability;
- uncertainty and out-of-distribution detection;
- privacy and retention;
- versioning of firmware, preprocessing, and models.

There is no validated cross-sport specification in the supplied evidence for an acceptable synchronization error, missingness rate, or labeling-quality threshold. Reported values are system-specific. The PE assessment study reduced an average IMU-to-rubric offset from 312 ms to 18 ms with DTW. EdgeFusionNet reports hardware-triggered sub-millisecond cross-modal alignment. Those results show what particular systems achieved; they do not establish one universal tolerance for every sport or teaching task.

Labels also have different meanings. A teacher rubric is an expert judgment. A force plate or marker-based motion-capture system may provide a biomechanical reference. A successful shot or race time is a performance outcome. A learner’s self-report is contextual evidence. The system must store the label provenance and avoid calling all of these “ground truth.”

The PE assessment study illustrates good practice. Three calibrated teachers independently scored all samples, achieved ICC(2,k) = 0.87, and used consensus labels with adjudication of low-agreement cases. Even so, the authors explicitly state that the model reproduces expert-level teacher scoring rather than objective biomechanical measurement. The same distinction should apply to any model trained on coach labels.

## 4. System construction and multimodal data-fusion architecture

### 4.1 Reference architecture

The proposed construction follows the six-stage architecture identified in the multimodal learning-analytics survey:

> acquisition and temporal alignment → preprocessing and quality control → modality-specific features → multimodal fusion → inference and learner modeling → pedagogical interpretation and feedback

This sequence should be implemented as modular services so that a new sport can replace a domain model or sensor adapter without rebuilding the entire system.

### 4.2 Stage 1: acquisition, identity, and consent

The acquisition layer should support interchangeable connectors for cameras, phones, IMUs, GPS or UWB, force platforms, pressure insoles, EMG, heart-rate devices, audio, LMS data, and structured self-report.

A sport-specific sensor configuration is preferable to maximal instrumentation. Optical motion capture can provide high-quality laboratory references, but surveys report calibration, synchronization, occlusion, scene size, and cost constraints. Wearables improve field portability but introduce drift, placement variability, and signal-quality problems. The 2024 motion-capture survey reports that large optical scenes can require more than 20 cameras and that documented systems have a maximum working range not exceeding 1,000 m². It also reports commercial UWB systems with dynamic indoor measurement errors below 0.5% of the working range in the reviewed examples. [Motion-capture survey](https://doi.org/10.3390/s24092947)

Every acquisition session should create a provenance record containing:

- participant or learner pseudonymous identifier;
- consent scope and withdrawal status;
- sport, task, venue, and session phase;
- device type, firmware, placement, calibration, and sampling rate;
- synchronization source and estimated clock error;
- data-quality flags;
- model and preprocessing versions;
- human annotations and their provenance.

The system should separate identifying data from movement and physiological data. A teacher may need to see a learner’s name, while a model-training service may need only a pseudonymous identifier and a consented feature record.

### 4.3 Stage 2: temporal alignment and quality control

The most consequential engineering error in multimodal systems is often not the classifier but the alignment of streams that describe different moments.

A suitable procedure is:

1. use hardware or network timestamps whenever possible;
2. perform device-specific latency correction;
3. resample to an analysis grid without erasing event peaks;
4. align continuous and discrete streams through event markers or DTW;
5. record residual synchronization error;
6. apply modality-specific quality flags;
7. preserve missingness rather than replacing all gaps with an unqualified interpolation.

The smart classroom design uses 30 Hz video, 100 Hz IMUs, and 1 Hz heart rate. It smooths video keypoints, filters IMU acceleration and angular velocity at 5 Hz, averages heart rate over five-second windows, interpolates missing heart-rate values, removes low-confidence transcripts, and normalizes features to the [0, 1] range. These are reported design choices, not universal preprocessing standards.

The PE assessment model uses complementary filtering, adaptive Kalman filtering, time-, frequency-, and time-frequency-domain features, quaternion joint angles, DTW, attention, and quality-sensitive gated fusion. The supplied article extraction omits several displayed equations. The report therefore preserves the described operations without reconstructing symbols that are not available in the extracted text.

Quality control should identify distinct failure modes:

- random frame dropout;
- contiguous bursts;
- single-axis loss;
- single-node failure;
- calibration drift;
- implausible values;
- occlusion;
- poor audio confidence;
- packet loss;
- device displacement.

This distinction matters because random missingness is easier to tolerate than a failed sensor that removes one whole anatomical region. EdgeFusionNet and the PE assessment model both show that multimodal redundancy can improve resilience, but neither result guarantees reliability under every operational failure.

### 4.4 Stage 3: feature extraction and representation

Feature extraction should preserve both sport-specific meaning and model flexibility.

Video may yield keypoints, joint angles, trajectories, object relations, gaze, and temporal phases. IMUs may yield acceleration peaks, angular velocity, orientation, jerk, smoothness, symmetry, spectral energy, and event timing. Physiological data may yield heart-rate zones, HRV, recovery trends, exertion timing, and individualized deviations from baseline. Audio and text may yield coach cues, learner questions, self-reported fatigue, pain, confidence, or motivation.

Models should not be forced to operate on a single representation. A pose graph can represent joint relationships; a recurrent model can represent temporal change; a transformer can model longer dependencies; a physics-informed model can constrain impossible movement; and a language model can verbalize structured findings.

The 2025 sports-biomechanics scoping review reports median accuracy of 87.50% for Random Forest studies and 91.00% for CNN video studies in its heterogeneous corpus. It also reports that only 43.84% of included studies demonstrated adequate validation procedures. These values are descriptive study-level summaries, not evidence that CNNs are universally superior. Traditional models remain useful with smaller datasets, lower computational budgets, or stronger interpretability requirements. [Sports biomechanics scoping review](https://doi.org/10.3390/bioengineering12080887)

### 4.5 Stage 4: multimodal fusion

Fusion is the mechanism that combines modalities. The principal alternatives are:

| Fusion approach | Construction | Strength | Limitation and appropriate use |
|---|---|---|---|
| Early fusion | Concatenate raw or low-level data before representation learning | Can learn direct cross-modal interactions | Highly sensitive to timing, scaling, missing channels, and dimensionality |
| Intermediate fusion | Learn modality-specific representations, then combine them before prediction | Balances specialization and interaction modeling | Requires careful architecture and sufficient data |
| Late fusion | Combine modality-specific predictions or scores | Robust to missing modalities and easier to audit | May miss fine-grained relationships between streams |
| Hybrid or adaptive fusion | Use modality encoders, attention, gates, and quality-dependent weighting | Can model complementarity while responding to reliability | More complex, harder to validate, and vulnerable to overfitting |

This taxonomy is established in multimodal machine learning. Boulahia and colleagues distinguish early, intermediate, and late fusion and caution that hand-built late-fusion rules can be biased under real-world variation. The 2026 multimodal-learning survey similarly emphasizes that fusion strategies should be evaluated under channel dropout, device shift, and incomplete data rather than only on complete laboratory samples. [Boulahia et al.](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00138-021-01249-8) [Future Internet survey](https://doi.org/10.3390/fi18030115)

The proposed SITLGS should use hybrid fusion by default when modalities have different sampling rates, different reliability, and different pedagogical meanings. A practical arrangement is:

- modality-specific encoders for video, IMU, physiology, audio, and text;
- temporal alignment before cross-modal interaction;
- attention within each modality;
- cross-modal attention for complementary evidence;
- a gate that reweights streams according to quality and task;
- an uncertainty head that estimates whether the result is safe to present as guidance;
- an ablation and missingness evaluator that quantifies what each modality adds.

The modality weight should not be interpreted as a universal causal explanation. In the PE assessment model, the IMU stream received higher weight for standing long jump and sprint, while rubric evidence was more important for basketball dribbling. This is pedagogically plausible because the rubric captures coordination and form that the IMUs cannot fully observe. It is not proof that attention weights always correspond to human explanations.

### 4.6 Stage 5: inference, learner modeling, and domain modeling

The inference layer should use different models for different decisions.

Recognition models identify action, phase, or error. CNNs and pose models are suitable for video; CNN-RNN combinations handle spatiotemporal patterns; GCNs represent skeletal or player relationships; transformers model longer sequences; and lightweight temporal convolution or recurrent models can support edge inference.

Prediction models estimate performance, fatigue, recovery, load, or risk. Random Forest, XGBoost, Bayesian recurrent networks, and physics-informed models may be appropriate depending on sample size, interpretability, and outcome. Injury-risk outputs should be probabilistic decision support, not diagnoses.

Learner-state models estimate mastery and progression. Knowledge tracing, Bayesian updating, state-space models, and sequence models can represent the probability that a learner has mastered a skill component. The BDEN educational framework illustrates a large-scale attention-enhanced BiLSTM knowledge-tracing approach using 4.2 million interactions from 18,600 learners. Its reported 91.4% accuracy and 0.947 AUC are educational analytics results, not sports evidence, but the underlying pattern is transferable: interactions update estimated mastery, and mastery estimates inform recommendations. [BDEN knowledge-tracing framework](https://doi.org/10.17485/ijst/v19i30.1058)

The proposed learner model should include:

- baseline technical and physical profile;
- current mastery by skill component;
- recent errors and corrected errors;
- response to feedback;
- fatigue, recovery, and workload state;
- confidence, motivation, perceived exertion, pain, and self-report;
- preferred feedback modality;
- accessibility needs;
- goals and constraints;
- uncertainty and data-quality history.

The domain model should include:

- skill hierarchy and prerequisites;
- movement phases and event definitions;
- acceptable technique ranges rather than one rigid ideal;
- task difficulty and environmental constraints;
- common errors and their likely causes;
- drills and progressions;
- safety rules and escalation conditions;
- rubric dimensions and their provenance;
- coach- or teacher-approved explanations.

The pedagogical model should decide how to act on the learner model. It may use a constrained Markov decision process, as in the track-and-field system, but safety constraints must dominate performance rewards. A policy should not select a harder task merely because it maximizes short-term performance if the learner is fatigued, in pain, or uncertain.

### 4.7 Stage 6: tutoring services and feedback delivery

The tutoring service should convert a model output into an instructional action. A useful feedback object contains:

- the observed event;
- confidence and data-quality status;
- the relevant skill component;
- the comparison or criterion used;
- the likely error or opportunity;
- one actionable cue;
- a drill or practice constraint;
- the reason for the suggestion;
- an option to request human review.

Language models may help phrase this object, but they should not invent the underlying biomechanical diagnosis. Retrieval from a validated sport knowledge graph, coach-authored library, or approved curriculum should ground any generated explanation.

The interface should support:

- athlete or learner mobile access;
- teacher and coach dashboards;
- session-level and longitudinal views;
- visual replay with overlays;
- audio or text cues;
- optional haptic feedback;
- AR or VR where the hardware and context justify it;
- explicit uncertainty and “insufficient data” states;
- coach override and annotation;
- an audit trail of recommendations and overrides.

### 4.8 Edge-cloud deployment

The evidence supports a hybrid edge-cloud architecture, not an assumption that all data should be centralized.

Edge computing is appropriate for:

- low-latency action recognition;
- immediate safety or quality alerts;
- local preprocessing;
- data minimization;
- operation during intermittent connectivity;
- privacy-sensitive raw-video handling.

Cloud services are appropriate for:

- longitudinal learner modeling;
- model training;
- population-level analysis;
- secure backup;
- policy and content management;
- cross-session reporting;
- carefully controlled model updates.

The smart classroom system places lightweight recognition and feedback at the edge and long-term personalization in the cloud. EdgeFusionNet uses adaptive offloading and reports sub-32 ms P95 latency at 5 Mbps uplink. The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security similarly describes edge AI as commonly hybrid: local inference may coexist with cloud model updates, orchestration, telemetry, or fallback. It warns that edge processing does not automatically guarantee privacy and that hardware, energy, and fleet lifecycle costs must be included. [Canadian edge-AI guidance](https://www.cyber.gc.ca/en/guidance/securely-deploying-ai-network-edge-itsp80101)

A feedback-latency condition reported in the CoachXNet design is:

$`\tau_{\mathrm{fb}}\leq T_{\mathrm{motion}}/2=1/(2f_{\mathrm{motion}})`$.

This is a design stability bound, not an empirically universal requirement. It expresses the practical principle that corrective feedback should arrive within the relevant movement cycle and should not cause oscillatory corrections between successive attempts.

### 4.9 Interoperability, security, and auditability

The system should expose documented interfaces for:

- device and gateway ingestion;
- timestamp and calibration metadata;
- learner and session identity;
- sport-skill ontologies;
- LMS integration;
- coach and teacher annotations;
- model and policy versions;
- audit records;
- approved exports;
- deletion and correction requests.

A 2026 standards-first rehabilitation framework proposes profiles for device-to-gateway, gateway-to-edge, edge-to-cloud, model and policy updates, and auditability. It also proposes edge-first minimization and federated or incremental learning. This is a deployment blueprint rather than empirical conformance evidence. No supplied study demonstrates interoperability across a broad set of devices, learning platforms, electronic health records, and APIs. [Standards-first edge-cloud framework](https://doi.org/10.1109/mcomstd.2026.3687308)

Security controls should include encryption in transit and at rest, device identity, access control, segmentation, secure updates, anomaly detection, logging, backup, vulnerability management, and independent testing. The Canadian guidance recommends confidence, latency, and decision logs and requires accessible override or independent shutdown mechanisms for safety-relevant edge systems. FIA guidance similarly recommends encryption, access audits, penetration testing, intrusion detection, and vulnerability assessments for biometric systems, while warning that consumer-device accuracy may depend heavily on manufacturer claims. [FIA biometric guidance](https://www.fia.com/sites/default/files/fia_guidelines_for_the_collection_and_usage_of_biometric_data_in_motor_sport_eng_2021.pdf)

The supplied evidence does not include system-specific threat modeling, penetration-test results, or cybersecurity conformance results for the proposed SITLGS. Those should be treated as deployment requirements, not as established properties.

## 5. Intelligent tutoring and learning-guidance applications

### 5.1 The closed-loop sports-learning workflow

A practical session can be organized as follows.

#### 1. Plan

The system receives the learner’s goal, sport, current mastery, recent performance, workload, recovery information, injury history where lawfully available, and constraints. The coach or teacher confirms the objective and selects the acceptable feedback mode.

The Frontiers in Digital Health analysis describes a six-stage AI-coach workflow: planning, initiation, introduction, monitoring, adapting, and conclusion. Historical performance, physiological indicators, injury history, and goals inform the plan; a post-session report updates the ability model and future plan. This is a useful conceptual sequence, but the article is normative rather than a controlled validation of every stage. [AI-coach workflow analysis](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/digital-health/articles/10.3389/fdgth.2026.1781352/full)

#### 2. Initiate

The system checks device status, consent, calibration, connectivity, and quality. It should tell the user when a modality is missing or unreliable. A learner should not be given a precise-looking score derived from a disconnected sensor without a warning.

#### 3. Introduce

The tutor presents the target movement, tactical objective, or practice constraint through a teacher demonstration, video, 3D avatar, AR overlay, or textual explanation. The domain model supplies the relevant criteria. The learner may select a simpler or more challenging variant when appropriate.

#### 4. Observe and recognize

The system segments the attempt and estimates movement phase, action, technique features, and relevant physiological or contextual state. It should distinguish recognition from judgment. “The elbow angle differed from the reference” is not equivalent to “the movement was wrong”; the latter requires sport-specific context and pedagogical interpretation.

#### 5. Diagnose and explain

The system combines the learner model, domain model, and current evidence. It identifies a small number of actionable priorities rather than presenting every detected deviation. If confidence is low, data conflict across modalities, or the task is outside the training distribution, it should request coach review.

#### 6. Provide feedback and adapt

Feedback may be concurrent, terminal within the session, or delayed. It may be visual, spoken, haptic, textual, or embodied in AR or VR. The system can select the next drill, modify repetitions or rest, adjust difficulty, or postpone progression based on current learning and recovery.

#### 7. Review and update

At session end, the learner receives a progress summary and reflection prompt. The coach receives trends, unresolved errors, disagreement cases, and safety flags. The system stores the response to the intervention, not only the original movement, so that future recommendations can learn whether a cue or drill actually helped.

### 5.2 Skill assessment and action recognition

Skill assessment is the most developed application area.

The BMC PE model maps IMU signals and teacher rubrics to four-tier assessment. Its 91.3% result is meaningful because it uses participant-wise splitting, repeated random seeds, leave-one-school-out analysis, and inter-rater reliability. Its limitation is equally important: it reproduces expert scoring.

The track-and-field system combines action classification, quantitative performance prediction, uncertain trajectory forecasting, and injury-risk classification. Its technique F1 ranged from 0.88 for shot put to 0.94 for long jump, overall accuracy was 93.7%, and feedback latency was 67 ± 12 ms in the reported evaluation. These are model and system endpoints, not direct measures of learning.

BoxingPro shows how high-speed actions require complementary sensing. Vision can represent posture but may miss acceleration and velocity; IMUs can capture rapid kinematic detail but commonly identify the action without explaining how to improve it. Combining the two with an LLM produces a more contextual feedback object. The expert rating above 4/5 supports perceived quality, but not learning gain.

The PE system based on RGB video and AlphaPose keypoints demonstrates a lower-cost alternative. It fuses RGB and skeletal features, then uses joint-position and angular deviations to map errors to heatmaps and drills. Its reported accuracy and edge performance are preliminary, and the authors explicitly state that the evidence does not validate instructional effectiveness. [RGB and skeletal PE feedback model](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12997927/)

### 5.3 Technique analysis and error correction

Technique analysis becomes useful when the system links a detected deviation to a teachable correction.

For basketball shooting, a system may identify shoulder elevation or unstable elbow angles, visualize the affected joints, and recommend slow-motion demonstrations, partial-range drills, or pause-and-hold practice. For table tennis, it may connect stroke type, racket acceleration, trunk rotation, and coach-supplied suggestions. For badminton, it may compare contact point, footwork, sound, and landing with coach-defined criteria. For golf, Sportsbox AI presents 3D swing measurement, goals, instant feedback, and AI explanations, but its underlying sensing and fusion design are not publicly specified in the supplied product evidence.

The system should prioritize error explanations that are:

- specific enough to act upon;
- limited to one or two high-value corrections;
- linked to observable evidence;
- phrased in learner-appropriate language;
- compatible with the learner’s current skill;
- reversible if the coach rejects the interpretation.

Similarity scores and expert comparisons can support learning, but direct imitation of an elite performer may be inappropriate. Anthropometry, injury history, style, tactical intention, and task constraints can make a learner’s successful movement different from a reference exemplar.

### 5.4 Personalized instruction and adaptive training plans

Personalization should operate at several levels.

At the content level, the system chooses a skill or drill. At the difficulty level, it adjusts task complexity, speed, range, resistance, or environmental pressure. At the dosage level, it changes repetitions, rest, intensity, and session duration. At the feedback level, it chooses whether the learner needs a visual cue, verbal explanation, demonstration, question, or human intervention.

The smart classroom system uses a long-term performance index and phase thresholds to select 3–5 training items, adjust repetitions and rest based on physiological load, and use attendance and recovery to recommend frequency. The track-and-field system formalizes content optimization as a constrained Markov decision process. These are reported mechanisms, but their policy safety and long-term effects require prospective evaluation.

The system should not equate personalization with constant adaptation. Excessive changes can prevent learners from understanding cause and effect. A stable practice block may be pedagogically preferable when the goal is consolidation. Adaptation should be constrained by sport knowledge, the learner’s goal, safety rules, and coach approval.

### 5.5 Real-time and delayed feedback

The comparative feedback study by Sigrist and colleagues involved 24 naïve participants learning rowing in virtual reality with visual, audiovisual, or visuohaptic feedback. All groups reduced velocity and spatial error at retention, and audiovisual feedback supported velocity-profile learning more than visuohaptic feedback. The study shows that feedback modality can affect what is learned, but it did not establish transfer to other sports or rehabilitation. [Sigrist et al.](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00221-014-4167-7)

Real-time feedback is appropriate when:

- the correction concerns an observable feature of the current movement;
- the learner can process the cue without losing attention;
- the latency is short relative to the movement;
- the error is safe to correct immediately.

Delayed feedback is appropriate when:

- multiple attempts should be compared;
- the learner should reflect before receiving the answer;
- the issue concerns fatigue, recovery, or longitudinal trends;
- immediate interruption would disrupt tactical or perceptual learning.

A system should allow the coach or teacher to choose the feedback schedule. The same model output may be delivered as a simple cue during practice, a replay with explanation during a break, and a trend report after a training block.

### 5.6 Motivation, adherence, and social support

AI tutoring cannot be evaluated only by recognition accuracy because learning depends on willingness to practice.

The speed-skating study found that AI-assisted and Big-Unit teaching improved 500 m performance more than conventional instruction over eight weeks. It also found strong changes across 13 psychological outcomes, while mediation analysis suggested that motivation and self-efficacy were indirect pathways and direct technical impact remained dominant. The intact-class design means the result is not definitive causal evidence.

The REVERIE trial reported more than 90% median compliance in both sports groups and six-month gains in well-being, self-efficacy, and willingness to participate. Its VR environment may have increased novelty, social engagement, or perceived support; the study does not isolate which component caused the outcomes.

The academic student-athlete ITS study provides a useful caution. Completion improved after adding device choice, teacher interaction, supportive animation, and adaptive difficulty. The improvement cannot be attributed to the algorithm alone because the redesign also changed duration, interface, human support, and task selection.

A sports SITLGS should therefore log:

- voluntary practice frequency;
- completion and abandonment;
- feedback acceptance or rejection;
- perceived usefulness;
- motivation and autonomy;
- workload and cognitive burden;
- coach or teacher contact;
- adverse reactions or anxiety;
- sustained participation after novelty fades.

### 5.7 Safety and injury-risk guidance

Injury support should be treated as a safety-critical decision-support function.

A 2026 review organizes injury management into detection, evaluation, rehabilitation, monitoring, and return-to-sport assessment. It describes multimodal combinations such as IMU kinematics with LSTM or transformer models for ACL-risk probability, HRV and EMG with ensemble models for fatigue, video pose with CNN and GCN models for asymmetry, and training load with XGBoost for injury-likelihood scores. It also emphasizes that noise, sensor variability, inconsistent labels, and population shift limit generalization. [Multimodal AI for sports injury prediction](https://www.jhse.es/index.php/jhse/article/download/integrating-multimodal-ai-technologies-sports-injury-prediction/185)

The SITLGS may provide:

- a low-confidence warning that movement quality has changed;
- a request to reduce intensity and consult staff;
- a comparison with the learner’s own baseline;
- a rehabilitation exercise-monitoring summary;
- a return-to-sport evidence dashboard for qualified professionals.

It should not diagnose an injury, authorize return to play, or override pain, medical assessment, or athlete disclosure. Predictive validity and intervention effectiveness are different. A model may identify a risk pattern without reducing injury incidence, and an alert may be harmful if it produces unnecessary restriction or false reassurance.

### 5.8 Coach and teacher decision support

The system should reduce administrative and observational burden without transferring professional accountability to an opaque model.

A teacher dashboard may show:

- class-level skill distribution;
- students with the largest week-to-week change;
- students whose sensor evidence and rubric score disagree;
- confidence and missingness;
- suggested small-group drills;
- a replay and explanation for selected learners.

A coach dashboard may show:

- athlete-specific technical priorities;
- workload and recovery trends;
- comparison with personal baseline;
- response to the last intervention;
- uncertainty and alternate interpretations;
- training-plan options rather than one compulsory prescription.

Hudl demonstrates the value of clips, annotations, and messaging in real coaching workflows. The SITLGS should integrate with such workflows rather than require coaches to operate a separate technical console.

## 6. Evaluation design and application evidence

### 6.1 Evaluation dimensions

A credible evaluation must separate technical performance from educational effectiveness.

| Evaluation domain | Required measures | Appropriate comparison | Evidence currently available |
|---|---|---|---|
| Technical recognition | Accuracy, precision, recall, Macro-F1, confusion matrix, calibration, robustness | Single-modality, fusion variants, expert or instrument reference | Stronger evidence for narrow tasks; metrics are not standardized |
| Real-time operation | Median and tail latency, throughput, energy, packet loss, uptime | Edge-only, cloud-only, hybrid, different connectivity | Several prototypes report latency; lifecycle and uptime evidence is scarce |
| Personalization | Recommendation relevance, mastery estimation, adaptation quality, uncertainty | Fixed plan, population plan, human plan, ablation of learner model | Mostly early-stage or indirect evidence |
| Learning | Immediate gain, skill improvement, retention, transfer, delayed performance | Conventional teaching, video, non-intelligent technology, human coaching | Positive but heterogeneous evidence; sustained transfer is uncommon |
| Behavior and experience | Engagement, adherence, motivation, usability, trust, cognitive load | Baseline activity, alternative interface, human support | Some RCT, survey, and formative evidence |
| Coaching operations | Preparation time, review time, workload, override rate, adoption, training needs | Existing workflow or paper process | Major evidence gap |
| Safety and equity | False alerts, missed risks, adverse events, subgroup calibration, accessibility | Professional assessment and subgroup baselines | Governance requirements are better developed than outcome evidence |

### 6.2 Technical evidence

The BMC PE assessment model reports 91.3 ± 0.4% overall accuracy, compared with 82.7 ± 0.6% for IMU-only and 79.4 ± 0.8% for rubric-only baselines. It reduced temporal offset from 312 ms to 18 ms and achieved 43.2 ms single-sample inference. Under 30% frame-level random missingness, fusion accuracy remained 85.6 ± 0.5%; under whole-node failure it fell to 81.4 ± 0.8%. Leave-one-school-out accuracy was 88.1 ± 1.3%, showing a meaningful but bounded cross-institution drop. These results are unusually complete for a PE prototype, but the model remains within-population and teacher-label dependent. [BMC PE assessment model](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13102-026-01792-9)

EdgeFusionNet reports 93.6 ± 0.4% accuracy and Macro-F1 of 0.927 ± 0.005 across seven table-tennis strokes, 90.4 ± 2.3% leave-one-subject-out accuracy, and 91.8 ± 0.7% in uncontrolled gymnasium conditions. Its sub-32 ms P95 latency at 5 Mbps uplink is operationally relevant because it addresses connectivity rather than assuming a perfect network. Its field comparison with 12 athletes per arm and 30 sessions offers more ecological evidence than a static dataset, although it remains sport-specific. [EdgeFusionNet](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-58591-y)

The smart classroom system reports 89.4–93.2% recognition accuracy and 176–180 ms edge response time among 45 adult college students. Enabling personalized cloud analysis reportedly increased accuracy by about 3.4 percentage points, reduced response time by approximately 10.8 ms, and raised satisfaction from 3.9 to 4.5 on a five-point scale. These are useful system endpoints, but the comparison was not a randomized educational study and did not measure retention or transfer.
