[Smart classroom system](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01082-w)

The aerobic-gymnastics study demonstrates why modality count should not be equated with quality. Its video-and-motion CNN-RNN stream achieved 96.4% accuracy, whereas five-modality fusion achieved 93.7%, with 78 ms latency and 94.1% operational stability. Additional modalities did not improve the reported accuracy under those conditions. This may reflect noise, misalignment, redundant information, insufficient training data, or an outcome better captured by video and motion alone. [Aerobic-gymnastics system](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-62084-3)

The technical comparison also contains reporting contradictions. CoachXNet reports 94.1% accuracy and 32 ms average latency in one passage, but 94.6% on SportsPose, 92.8% on AthletePose3D, and 27.8 ms elsewhere. SportSkills reports different video and clip totals across sections. Hang-Time HAR reports 10 activities in its summary and 15 classes in its table. These discrepancies do not prove that the systems are invalid, but they prevent confident cross-study ranking.

### 6.3 Educational and behavioral evidence

The evidence for learning outcomes is more encouraging than the evidence for generalization, but it is not uniform.

The PoseSync Vitality randomized trial included 120 undergraduates and compared AI-supported Tai Chi instruction with video instruction under the same curriculum and practice dose. It reported larger performance gains, higher personalization and interface ratings, and posttest consistency advantages, with retention assessed after two weeks. This is direct evidence that pose-based tutoring can outperform passive video instruction under one controlled course condition. The supplied evidence does not provide the exact effect sizes or establish transfer beyond the routine studied. [PoseSync Vitality](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10639-026-14132-8)

The track-and-field study randomized 312 students to traditional or machine-learning-optimized instruction for 40 hours over 16 weeks. The optimized group reached proficiency 27.3% faster and had a reported 41.2% reduction in injury likelihood. Its held-out technical results were strong, but the interpretation of injury effects requires caution because injury likelihood may depend on exposure, reporting, baseline differences, and the operational definition of injury. [Track-and-field intelligent teaching](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-20745-9)

The REVERIE three-arm trial involved an eight-week sports intervention and a six-month follow-up. The main text reports benefits in standing long jump, self-efficacy, self-esteem, well-being, sleep, eating behavior, and sports willingness compared with physical sports. The existence of a follow-up is valuable because immediate posttest performance does not establish durable learning. However, the source reports 227 participants in the abstract and 240 enrolled in the main text; this must be resolved before using the result in a pooled calculation. [REVERIE](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1038/s41591-025-03724-5)

The speed-skating study involved 129 adolescents, three intact classes, 24 sessions over eight weeks, and baseline, mid-intervention, and post-intervention assessments. Both AI-assisted and Big-Unit teaching improved 500 m performance more than conventional teaching. Motivation, self-efficacy, resilience, and anxiety-related measures also changed, but intact-class allocation means teaching method and class context were partly confounded. [Speed-skating study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12907373/)

A 2025 controlled pedagogical study of AR-supported sports exercise reported greater precision and higher correct-technique retention after two weeks in the experimental group. The supplied evidence does not provide the full sample and effect-size details needed for a precise comparison. This is an example of why a claim of “better learning” should always include the outcome definition, baseline, duration, and delayed-test design. [AR sports-exercise study](https://doi.org/10.47197/retos.v73.117751)

The meta-analytic evidence is positive but heterogeneous. A 2026 review of 39 studies, including 17 quantitative studies, reported Hedges’ $`g = 0.67`$, 95% CI [0.51, 0.83], $`p \lt  .001`$, with $`I^2 = 58\%`$. Technical performance had the largest subgroup estimate at $`g = 0.74`$, followed by tactical, psychological, injury-prevention or rehabilitation, and physical performance outcomes. [Journal of Human Sport and Exercise review](https://www.jhse.es/index.php/jhse/article/view/ai-assisted-coaching-sports-performance)

A different 2026 systematic review included 15 studies, six in meta-analysis, and reported SMD = 3.15 with $`I^2 = 98\%`$. The very high heterogeneity makes the pooled magnitude unstable and limits direct interpretation. [Hanief et al.](https://journal.rezkimedia.or.id/index.php/jaieli/article/view/753)

These positive pooled results must be reconciled with a 2026 scoping review of sports-AI research that included 32 publications and found that none demonstrated sustained decision impact or attributable improvement in athlete, educational, sports-medicine, or organizational outcomes. The apparent conflict is explained by different evidence universes and outcome definitions. Meta-analyses combine short-term or intermediate performance effects across varied interventions; the scoping review asks whether a system produced sustained, attributable real-world impact with prospective or independent validation. Both findings can be true: some interventions improve measured outcomes, while the field as a whole lacks mature evidence of durable system-level impact. [Sports-AI scoping review](https://ijpefs.org/index.php/ijpefs/article/view/833)

### 6.4 Evaluation of LLM-mediated coaching

Language-based tutoring requires a separate evaluation standard. A 2025 JMIR scoping review included 20 LLM-based exercise and health-coaching studies. The median Evaluation Rigor Score was 2.5 out of 5; 55% were classified as low rigor, only two achieved the highest score, and 45% reported inter-rater reliability. Most studies relied on human ratings, while only 40% used automated metrics. Existing benchmarks such as SportQA, SCBench, and SPORTU assess knowledge or action description, not safe, personalized, fatigue-adapted, real-time corrective coaching. [JMIR LLM coaching review](https://www.jmir.org/2025/1/e79217/)

An LLM component in the SITLGS should therefore be evaluated for:

- factual and biomechanical correctness;
- grounding in approved domain content;
- actionability;
- appropriateness to learner level;
- harmful or unsafe recommendations;
- consistency across paraphrased prompts;
- response to missing or conflicting data;
- escalation behavior;
- accessibility and language quality;
- effects on learning, not only response preference.

The language model should not receive credit for the accuracy of a sensor model. The two layers should be evaluated separately and together.

### 6.5 User acceptance and adoption evidence

A 2025 survey of Romanian sports professionals used PLS-SEM to model perceived AI benefits, AI-application use, digital-technology use, and self-reported performance. The methods section reports 293 valid responses, while the Results section reports 214; this internal discrepancy prevents a simple sample-size interpretation. The reported associations—AI benefits to AI application use, AI application use to digital-technology use, and digital-technology use to performance—are cross-sectional survey relationships, not causal evidence that AI improved performance. [Romanian sports-professional survey](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/15/16/8853)

A 2026 systematic review of digital coaching included 15 eligible studies from 2021–2025 and concluded that technical accuracy was consistently high but evidence for long-term coaching effectiveness, usability, implementation, and ethical governance remained thin. This aligns with the operational evidence: technical systems are often easier to evaluate than whether coaches continue using them, whether workload falls, or whether organizations retain them. [Digital-coaching systematic review](https://jrti.eloracenter.org/jrti/article/view/6907)

### 6.6 A defensible evaluation protocol for the proposed system

A future SITLGS evaluation should pre-specify:

- population, sport, age range, skill level, sex, and accessibility characteristics;
- task definitions and label provenance;
- intervention dose and duration;
- primary and secondary outcomes;
- baseline and comparator;
- inclusion and exclusion criteria;
- missing-data policy;
- athlete- or participant-wise splits;
- time-forward and external validation;
- analysis plan and stopping rules;
- safety escalation and adverse-event reporting.

Technical evaluation should include precision, recall, Macro-F1, calibration, confusion by skill level, latency distribution rather than only average latency, packet loss, energy, and robustness under realistic missingness. Accuracy alone is insufficient for imbalanced injury or safety outcomes.

Educational evaluation should include immediate skill performance, delayed retention, transfer to a new context, and, where appropriate, competition or authentic-task performance. The system should be compared with conventional instruction, passive video, a single-modality tool, and human-coach practice where feasible.

Behavioral evaluation should measure adherence, motivation, perceived autonomy, cognitive load, usability, trust, and feedback acceptance. Operational evaluation should measure coach preparation time, review time, override rate, training requirements, uptime, device burden, and cost. Safety evaluation should measure false reassurance, unnecessary alerts, adverse events, and the correctness of escalation.

The evidence does not support inventing one minimum accuracy, latency, or learning-gain threshold for every sport. Acceptance criteria must be set before a pilot in relation to the decision risk and pedagogical objective. A 43.2 ms assessment model, a 176–180 ms classroom system, and a sub-32 ms table-tennis feedback system may all be suitable for different tasks.

## 7. Deployment, ethics, governance, and limitations

### 7.1 Privacy and data classification

Sports tutoring systems may process personal identifiers, biometric data, health data, location, behavioral patterns, voice, video, and inferred psychological or performance characteristics.

The UK Information Commissioner’s Office defines biometric data as personal data resulting from technical processing of physical, physiological, or behavioral characteristics that allow or confirm unique identification. It treats health data broadly, including injury, disease risk, medical history, medical-device results, and fitness-tracker data. Inferred information can also become special-category data when processing intends to infer a special category or treat a person differently on that basis. [ICO special-category guidance](https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/lawful-basis/special-category-data/what-is-special-category-data/)

The European Data Protection Board states that an AI model trained with personal data cannot automatically be considered anonymous. Anonymity must be assessed case by case, including whether information can be extracted directly or probabilistically using means reasonably likely to be used. The EDPB’s legitimate-interest test requires identification of a lawful, clearly articulated, real and present interest; necessity; and balancing against the data subject’s rights and freedoms. [EDPB Opinion 28/2024](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/system/files/2024-12/edpb_opinion_202428_ai-models_en.pdf)

For the SITLGS, meaningful consent should include:

- what data are collected;
- which features are inferred;
- who can access raw data, derived data, and reports;
- whether data train future models;
- how long data are retained;
- whether data leave the institution or country;
- how consent can be withdrawn;
- what happens to participation or selection if monitoring is refused;
- how data can be corrected, exported, or deleted.

Consent is especially difficult in professional, scholarship-dependent, school, and selection settings. The athlete-data sovereignty commentary describes how institutional systems combine medical, performance, and commercial modules, making data lineage and deletion difficult. It also cites collective-bargaining examples in which athlete consent, access, secondary use, and joint oversight receive explicit treatment. [Athlete data sovereignty commentary](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12745375/)

### 7.2 Children and young people

Youth sport requires heightened safeguards because children may not understand long-term data consequences and may have limited power to refuse monitoring.

The NSPCC’s 2026 guidance states that in the United Kingdom, children can generally consent to personal-data processing for online information-society services from age 13, while under-13 consent requires a parent or carer. It states that biometric data require parental consent regardless of age and that children can refuse. Where children are likely to access a service, the ICO Children’s Code requires high privacy by default, child-friendly language, geolocation and profiling turned off unless necessary, and no privacy-weakening nudges. [NSPCC youth-sport AI guidance](https://sport.nspcc.org.uk/media/nktm0suh/using-ai-in-youth-sport.pdf)

Procurement for youth sport should require a Data Protection Impact Assessment, appropriate data hosting and encryption, disclosure of training-data representation for youth, girls, and disabled participants, model limitations, confirmation about future model training, bias testing, a named security contact, and an incident-response plan. These are UK-centered examples; other jurisdictions may impose different obligations.

### 7.3 Fairness and bias

Bias can enter through sensor accuracy, body morphology, camera viewpoint, teacher rubrics, missing data, participation access, labels, and the outcome chosen for optimization.

A model trained mostly on adult male athletes may misinterpret women, children, older adults, para-athletes, or athletes with atypical anthropometry. A model trained in one country may encode local coaching norms. A model trained on successful elite movement may incorrectly treat developmental variation as error. A model trained on teacher scores may reproduce shared teacher bias even when inter-rater reliability is high.

Fairness evaluation should include:

- subgroup accuracy, precision, recall, and calibration;
- error by sex, age, skill level, disability, body type, and sport;
- false-alert and missed-alert rates;
- cross-site and cross-device performance;
- label disagreement by subgroup;
- accessibility of feedback;
- the effect of missing or unavailable modalities;
- human review of disputed outputs.

The Frontiers in Digital Health analysis gives illustrative examples of systems trained on European or U.S. data producing less suitable recommendations for Asian athletes, recommending activities based on popular trends rather than user capability, or failing to meet women’s needs when historical data are male-dominated. These examples are conceptual bias scenarios rather than empirical estimates, but they describe plausible failure mechanisms. [Frontiers in Digital Health analysis](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/digital-health/articles/10.3389/fdgth.2026.1781352/full)

The PE assessment prototype reported almost identical accuracy for boys and girls and relatively flat performance across age groups within its sample. This is encouraging but not sufficient to establish fairness because the model may still reproduce common biases in teacher labels. The authors themselves caution that expert-consensus training labels are not objective ground truth.

### 7.4 Explainability, contestability, and human oversight

Explainability must be linked to decisions rather than added as a decorative visualization. Coaches and teachers need to know:

- which modality was available;
- whether data quality was adequate;
- which movement phase influenced the output;
- which features or body regions contributed;
- what reference or rubric was used;
- how uncertain the model is;
- what alternative explanation is plausible;
- how to override the result.

An umbrella review of explainability in educational data mining found that none of the ten retained publications reported a metric for explanation quality or effectiveness. It also found no consensus algorithm that jointly optimizes predictive performance, explainability, and fairness. [EDM explainability review](https://educationaldatamining.org/edm2024/proceedings/2024.EDM-posters.104/index.html)

The SITLGS should therefore evaluate whether explanations improve teacher decisions, learner understanding, calibration of trust, and correction of errors. Attention weights and feature attributions may help audit a model, but they should not automatically be presented as causal explanations.

Human oversight should be active rather than nominal. Coaches and teachers should be able to reject, edit, defer, or annotate system outputs. Safety-relevant actions should require professional review. Learners should have a way to contest a score or recommendation. The system should preserve a record of overrides and use them to identify recurring model or rubric problems.

### 7.5 Reliability and failure modes

Failure modes include:

- camera occlusion or poor light;
- sensor displacement or calibration drift;
- packet loss and battery depletion;
- synchronization error;
- missing modalities;
- unusual movement or equipment;
- sport or venue shift;
- fatigue and stress not represented in the model;
- ambiguous teacher labels;
- hallucinated language-model explanations;
- excessive feedback and cognitive overload;
- false injury alerts;
- silent model updates;
- connectivity loss;
- unauthorized access.

The 2026 biosensing review emphasizes motion artefacts, inter-session variability, laboratory-to-field distribution shift, and overconfident predictions when contextual or psychosocial inputs are absent. It concludes that biosensor-based AI should support decision-making rather than operate as an autonomous coach. [Wearable biosensing and ML review](https://doi.org/10.3390/bios16020097)

A safe deployment should include a “no recommendation” state. If data quality is low, the system should say that it cannot confidently assess the action. It should not interpolate uncertainty away and present a precise score.

### 7.6 Infrastructure, interoperability, and economic feasibility

Edge deployment can reduce latency and data transfer, but it requires hardware management, energy, firmware updates, replacement, physical security, and local technical support. Cloud deployment simplifies centralized updates but creates connectivity, latency, data-residency, and recurring-service concerns.

The supplied evidence includes hardware examples—Intel i5 edge servers, Raspberry Pi, Jetson Nano, Jetson Xavier NX, A100 clusters, cameras, IMUs, force platforms, and VR headsets—but does not provide a comparable total-cost analysis. Procurement cost, maintenance, calibration, replacement, staff training, insurance, connectivity, and data storage are therefore unavailable as cross-system quantities.

Access is also an equity issue. The 2025 PE review found that 80% of included studies concerned higher education and 98% typically developing populations; only two studies addressed special populations. It also found that 86% of applications occurred in offline courses and 95% in-school, leaving after-school and non-formal contexts underexplored. [Frontiers in Public Health PE review](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2025.1626603)

A low-cost smartphone and one IMU may increase access but provide less information than a laboratory system. A high-end VR and multimodal platform may support richer training but exclude schools or communities without stable infrastructure. The system should offer capability tiers rather than define the fully instrumented configuration as the only valid form.

### 7.7 Regulatory and governance boundaries

The EU AI Act defines an AI system by its ability to infer predictions, content, recommendations, or decisions from inputs, with varying autonomy and possible adaptiveness after deployment. It also discusses biometric identification and related physiological or behavioral features. The applicable obligations depend on the system’s purpose, role, and jurisdiction; the definition alone does not determine a complete compliance pathway. [Regulation (EU) 2024/1689](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=OJ%3AL_202401689)

The GDPR applies in the European Union from 25 May 2018 and covers consent, security, impact assessment, access, erasure, and automated decision-making. National laws and sector-specific rules may add requirements. [GDPR legal text and guidance](https://gdpr-info.eu/)

FIA biometric guidance illustrates sport-specific governance. It requires homologation for biometric devices used in FIA competitions and recommends encryption, access auditing, penetration testing, intrusion detection, and vulnerability assessment. It also states that the guidelines are guidance rather than a legal obligation. This is a useful operational reference, not a universal rule for all sports. [FIA biometric-data guidelines](https://www.fia.com/sites/default/files/fia_guidelines_for_the_collection_and_usage_of_biometric_data_in_motor_sport_eng_2021.pdf)

## 8. Conclusions, implementation roadmap, and future research

### 8.1 Evidence-based judgment

A Sports Intelligent Tutoring and Learning Guidance System driven by multimodal data fusion is technically feasible and pedagogically promising when its scope is defined carefully.

The evidence is strongest for:

- recognizing and assessing narrowly defined actions;
- combining complementary movement and expert information;
- providing low-latency feedback in controlled or semi-controlled settings;
- supporting formative assessment;
- adapting task difficulty or training load under explicit constraints;
- improving selected short-term performance and engagement outcomes;
- reducing the burden of reviewing large amounts of movement data.

The evidence is weaker for:

- autonomous coaching;
- open-sport tactical tutoring;
- cross-sport and cross-population generalization;
- durable retention and transfer;
- independent external validation;
- reductions in actual injury incidence;
- sustained coach acceptance and workload reduction;
- institutional adoption and retention;
- total cost and economic feasibility;
- interoperability across vendors, LMS platforms, and health systems.

The correct conclusion is not that multimodal fusion automatically produces better learning. The correct conclusion is that multimodal evidence can improve the observability and personalization of sports learning when synchronization, labels, pedagogy, uncertainty, and human oversight are designed together.

### 8.2 Prioritized implementation roadmap

The following roadmap is a proposed implementation sequence, not a reported outcome.

#### Phase 1: establish purpose, governance, and user requirements

Select one sport, one learner population, and one instructional problem. Define whether the initial objective is skill assessment, technique feedback, adaptive practice, workload guidance, or safety support. Involve athletes, teachers, coaches, sport scientists, safeguarding staff, data-protection officers, and accessibility representatives.

Before collecting data, approve consent, retention, access, deletion, model-training, and human-override policies. For minors, complete the additional safeguarding and parental-consent requirements. The decision gate is a documented purpose, risk assessment, consent model, and user workflow.

#### Phase 2: define a benchmark and measurement protocol

Specify the target skill, outcome, reference standard, label provenance, sampling rates, synchronization method, missingness categories, and subgroup reporting. Collect a small but diverse calibration dataset across skill levels, body types, sex, age, environment, and relevant accessibility conditions.

Do not use a generic benchmark as a substitute for a sport-specific outcome. Establish baseline systems, such as video-only, IMU-only, rubric-only, fixed training, and conventional teaching. The decision gate is evidence that labels are reliable enough for the intended decision and that the measurement protocol can be repeated across sessions.

#### Phase 3: build a modular, uncertainty-aware prototype

Implement acquisition, quality control, temporal alignment, modality encoders, fusion, learner modeling, and feedback as separate modules. Start with one or two modalities that are demonstrably useful. Add a third modality only if ablation and missingness experiments show incremental value.

Use an edge component for immediate inference and a cloud or institutional component for longitudinal analysis. Include confidence, quality flags, a no-recommendation state, audit logs, and a human override from the first prototype. The decision gate is technical performance on participant-wise, time-forward, and simulated failure tests.

#### Phase 4: conduct a supervised classroom or training pilot

Deploy with a teacher or coach who can review every output. Measure not only accuracy and latency but also:

- learner understanding;
- feedback burden;
- motivation and autonomy;
- coach or teacher workload;
- override frequency;
- technical failures;
- accessibility;
- adverse events;
- data-governance compliance.

The pilot should compare the system with the actual local practice rather than an idealized baseline. A technically accurate model that increases teacher workload or learner confusion should not proceed directly to scale.

#### Phase 5: evaluate learning, retention, transfer, and safety

Use a randomized, matched, or stepped-wedge design appropriate to the setting. Prespecify immediate performance, delayed retention, transfer to a new task or environment, engagement, adherence, and safety outcomes. Use enough duration to observe whether effects persist after novelty.

For injury or health-related applications, involve qualified professionals and distinguish risk prediction from injury reduction. Do not use a surrogate technical endpoint as proof of clinical or safety benefit.

#### Phase 6: conduct independent and external validation

Test on new learners, schools, clubs, coaches, devices, venues, and seasons. Use leave-one-site-out and cross-sport transfer only when the target decision is genuinely intended to transfer. Report subgroup calibration, missingness, uncertainty, and failure modes.

The acceptance decision should be based on pre-specified thresholds agreed with practitioners and governance bodies. The supplied evidence does not support one universal threshold, so the threshold must reflect the harm of a false alert, missed error, or inappropriate training recommendation.

#### Phase 7: scale through interoperability and professional development

Integrate with existing LMS, athlete-management, video-review, and, where justified, health-record systems. Use stable data schemas, documented APIs, model versioning, export and deletion functions, and a clear support model.

Train teachers and coaches in sensor setup, uncertainty interpretation, explanation limits, bias, privacy, and override decisions. Professional development should make practitioners co-designers rather than passive recipients of algorithmic outputs.

### 8.3 Priority research agenda

#### Missing-data-resilient fusion

Future work should test modality dropout, structured sensor failure, calibration drift, connectivity loss, and adversarial or correlated missingness. Models should report whether they know when a missing modality changes the reliability of the recommendation.

#### Longitudinal learner models

Most systems recognize actions within sessions. Research should model how practice, fatigue, motivation, feedback, and context change mastery over weeks, months, and seasons. Learner models should distinguish temporary performance fluctuations from durable learning.

#### Retention and transfer

Studies should include delayed retention tests and transfer to new equipment, environments, opponents, tasks, or tactical conditions. Immediate posttest improvement should not be treated as equivalent to learning.

#### Cross-sport and cross-population generalization

A modular domain model may transfer between related sports, but the evidence must show where transfer works and where sport-specific retraining is necessary. Models should be evaluated across sex, age, disability, body morphology, skill level, cultural context, and resource setting.

#### Explainable and contestable feedback

Research should test whether feature attributions, attention maps, motion overlays, and natural-language explanations actually improve teacher decisions and learner understanding. Explanation quality should be measured rather than assumed.

#### Human–AI collaboration

The key question is not whether an AI can imitate a coach in a narrow task. It is whether the combined system improves decisions, reduces workload, preserves autonomy, and supports better relationships. Studies should measure coach trust, override quality, workload, professional learning, and responsibility allocation.

#### Safety and calibrated uncertainty

Sports tutors need calibrated probabilities, uncertainty-aware escalation, and robust no-action states. Research should connect technical uncertainty to practical decisions rather than reporting confidence as an isolated model metric.

#### Accessibility and inclusion

Systems should support athletes with disabilities, alternative movement patterns, language differences, low connectivity, and limited equipment. Accessibility should be designed into the interaction and feedback layers rather than added after model development.

#### Economic and institutional feasibility

Future studies should report total cost of ownership, staff time, maintenance, hardware replacement, data storage, training, licensing, and retention. Economic evidence is currently unavailable for comparable cross-system analysis.

#### Governance and athlete data sovereignty

Future deployment models should address portability, correction, deletion, secondary use, commercial licensing, collective bargaining, and the ability to refuse monitoring without unfair consequences. Athlete and learner representation should be built into governance.

## Closing judgment

The most defensible SITLGS is a modular, multimodal, edge-cloud, human-supervised learning system. Its value lies in connecting sensing to learner modeling and pedagogy: recognizing movement is necessary, but useful tutoring also requires sport knowledge, adaptive difficulty, meaningful feedback, longitudinal progress, safety constraints, and trusted human relationships.

The evidence already supports research and carefully supervised deployment in specific settings. It does not support treating any current system as a universally valid autonomous coach. Progress will depend less on adding modalities indiscriminately than on improving synchronization, data quality, learner modeling, calibrated uncertainty, external validation, accessibility, interoperability, and human–AI collaboration.
